strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: combining survival prediction, uncertainty quantification, and interpretable WSI representations. The proposed integration of patch-level GMM prototypes, component prototypes, and Gaussian random fuzzy-number evidence is conceptually interesting and reasonably original as a combination.

The method is presented with explicit equations and a useful three-stage overview. Experiments cover five TCGA cancer cohorts, use site-stratified five-fold cross-validation, and report discrimination and probabilistic-performance metrics.
DPsurv obtains the best reported mean C-index (0.685), IBS (0.288), and IBLL (0.862). The component assignment maps and representative prototypes could be useful exploratory tools for pathologists.
The appendix provides cohort sizes, baseline descriptions, optimization settings, and some derivations. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges sensitivity to prototype counts.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty/calibration claim is not adequately supported. Prediction-interval coverage is computed only on uncensored patients, which generally yields a selected and biased sample of event times. No censoring-adjusted coverage estimator, time-dependent calibration analysis, or external validation is provided. Moreover, coverage is reported without interval width or another sharpness measure, so the wider belief intervals can appear better calibrated trivially; the claim that they are both more calibrated and more precise is unsupported.

The survival comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Several baselines are substantially modified from their original settings, including removing genomics from UMSA, adding PCA/GMM processing to EVREG, and adapting classification methods to discrete survival. The appendix also says PANTHER uses a Cox loss while later saying it is adapted to discrete survival prediction. These inconsistencies make the very large IBS/IBLL gains difficult to interpret.

The reported predictive advantage is not statistically established. The mean C-index gain over PANTHER is only 0.018, fold variability is high (for example, 0.17 on LUAD), and no paired tests, confidence intervals for differences, or per-fold results are supplied. Calling the within-cohort experiments “cross-cancer evaluation” and inferring cross-cancer generalizability is inaccurate because no cross-cancer transfer experiment is performed.

There are important methodological ambiguities. The notation describes fitting slide-specific GMM parameters, yet component indices are subsequently treated as semantically aligned across patients. Initialization from shared prototypes does not guarantee such alignment after per-slide EM. Patch prototypes also disappear from the stated likelihood, and it is unclear whether covariances are full or diagonal despite the claimed 2d+1 representation. These details affect both validity and reproducibility.

The interpretation evidence is mainly a single qualitative example. The manuscript does not report the number of pathologists, review protocol, blinding, inter-rater agreement, or quantitative correspondence between prototypes and histologic labels. The proposed relative-risk score is merely within-slide min-max normalization of component means: it forces extrema to risks zero and one, is undefined when all means coincide, ignores uncertainty and mixture abundance, and does not establish component contribution or causal importance.

Several technical claims are imprecise. The paper alternately describes h as epistemic uncertainty and as evidential precision, although larger h makes the fuzzy evidence more precise. The rationale for penalizing h is therefore unclear. The provided C-index equation omits censoring/comparability conditions, and IBS is repeatedly treated as a pure calibration metric even though it combines calibration and discrimination.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims: no code or split identifiers are provided; random seeds, tissue segmentation and patch filtering, endpoint construction, evaluation integration horizons, validation-based hyperparameter selection, parameter constraints, and numerical implementation of interval inversion are missing. Dataset-specific prototype counts and learning rates appear manually selected without a documented nested validation protocol.

The clinical implications are overstated. Results come exclusively from retrospective TCGA cohorts, with no external cohort, subgroup/fairness analysis, prospective assessment, or formal discussion of deployment risks. Use of public de-identified data limits immediate ethical concern, but the manuscript lacks a clear ethics/data-governance statement and does not justify claims about treatment safety or clinical decision-making.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent combination of PANTHER-style GMM slide representations, component prototypes, and Gaussian random fuzzy numbers, producing both survival curves and belief/plausibility intervals.

Evaluation covers five public TCGA cohorts using site-stratified five-fold cross-validation and a shared UNI2-h feature extractor. DPsurv obtains the best reported mean C-index (0.685), IBS (0.288), and IBLL (0.862), although important protocol concerns limit what can be concluded from these numbers.

The component-assignment maps and prototype retrievals could be useful exploratory tools. Figure 2 gives an intuitive qualitative example connecting tissue morphology, prototype evidence, and predicted risk.

The manuscript is generally organized and supplies derivations, dataset sizes, baseline descriptions, and many training hyperparameters in the appendix. The authors also honestly acknowledge sensitivity to prototype counts.

Originality is moderate: the individual ingredients largely derive from PANTHER and prior GRFN survival models, but their component-wise evidential mixture is a potentially useful synthesis. weaknesses: Soundness: the central uncertainty claim is not convincingly evaluated. Figure 3 computes interval coverage only among uncensored subjects, a selected subset whose event-time distribution generally differs from the target population. No censoring-adjusted coverage estimator, time-dependent assessment, or comparison against competing uncertainty methods is provided. Consequently, the figure does not establish calibrated uncertainty under right censoring.

The interpretation of Figure 3 is technically incorrect: overcoverage means that intervals are conservative or too wide; it does not mean that the model avoids underestimating patient risk. A two-sided interval for log survival time cannot establish a directional tendency toward safer risk estimates. The associated clinical-treatment claim is unsupported.

The striking IBS/IBLL gains are difficult to trust as evidence for evidential uncertainty. IBS and IBLL score point survival distributions rather than epistemic intervals. Most baselines are adaptations of classification methods to four discrete time bins, whereas DPsurv produces a continuous GRFN-derived survival curve; the evaluation horizon, interpolation/extrapolation, censoring-estimator fitting, and risk-score construction are not specified. These choices can materially affect the reported metrics.

No ablation isolates the effects of patch prototypes, component prototypes, the mixture construction, evidential parameters, regularizers, or belief/plausibility mixing. There is also no sensitivity analysis for prototype counts, lambda, or other key choices, despite prototype-count sensitivity being the paper's principal acknowledged limitation. Thus, the evidence does not support the claimed mechanism.

The mixture has an insufficiently justified statistical interpretation. Per-slide GMM proportions describe patch prevalence, but the paper reinterprets them as probabilities selecting alternative patient-level survival distributions. It does not show that this produces a valid or identifiable patient survival model. Per-slide EM also creates possible label switching or component drift, yet component index c is assumed to have aligned semantics across patients when learning component-specific prototypes.

The claimed interpretability is supported almost entirely by a single qualitative figure. The paper gives no number of pathologists, annotation protocol, blinding, inter-rater agreement, quantitative localization assessment, or cohort-level validation. Retrieved prototypes and normalized within-slide risk scores demonstrate association, not faithful reasoning or clinically meaningful risk. Equation 13 is also undefined when all component means are equal.

Several methodological details needed for reproduction are missing or ambiguous: the number of survival bins for DPsurv, patch size and magnification, tissue segmentation, handling of multiple slides per patient, covariance parameterization, positivity constraints for variance/precision/decay parameters, stopping and model-selection rules, random seeds, exact splits, and the rule selecting fold-dependent K ranges. No code or split identifiers are supplied.

The empirical advantage in discrimination is modest and statistically unresolved: the mean C-index improves from 0.667 for PANTHER to 0.685, with large fold variability, including 0.17 standard deviation on LUAD. There are no paired statistical tests or confidence intervals, and no external-cohort validation.

Presentation contains consequential imprecision. The manuscript alternately describes h as epistemic uncertainty and as evidential precision, although larger h makes the fuzzy membership sharper. Its displayed C-index definition omits event/censoring comparability, and the claim that performance across cancer types shows generalizable tissue features is not supported because separate cohort-specific models and hyperparameters are used.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate for the clinical framing. It focuses narrowly on prototype counts and then speculates about diagnostic rules and treatment utility without prospective or external validation. It does not discuss TCGA selection bias, subgroup fairness, domain shift across laboratories, failure consequences, privacy/consent status, or the need for human oversight. These shortcomings make the clinical trustworthiness claims premature.

strengths: Soundness: DPsurV combines per-slide morphological mixtures, component prototypes, and Gaussian random fuzzy numbers into a coherent survival model. The resulting survival function is trained with a censoring-aware likelihood, and the manuscript provides derivations for the belief/plausibility functions and evidence mixture.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover five public TCGA cohorts using site-stratified five-fold cross-validation, a shared UNI2-h feature extractor, and discrimination and survival-scoring metrics. DPsurV obtains the best mean C-index (0.685), IBS (0.288), and IBLL (0.862), with particularly large calibration-score improvements on four cohorts.

Originality and significance: Although GMM slide representations, prototypes, and evidential survival modeling individually build on prior work, their component-wise integration is reasonably novel and potentially useful for uncertainty-aware computational pathology.

Presentation: The pipeline and its three interpretability levels are explained clearly. Figure 2 provides an intuitive trace from patch assignments through prototype evidence to spatial risk maps, and the appendix supplies dataset sizes, optimization settings, mathematical details, and an honest discussion of prototype-number sensitivity.

The use of public, de-identified cohorts and explicit acknowledgment of prototype sensitivity are positive. weaknesses: Soundness: The central uncertainty-calibration claim is not adequately established. Figure 3 computes interval coverage using only uncensored patients, which estimates coverage in an event-selected subset rather than coverage for the target survival population. A censoring-aware coverage estimator or an appropriate conformal-survival evaluation is needed. IBS and IBLL are useful proper prediction scores but do not, by themselves, validate the claimed epistemic/aleatory decomposition.

The comparison underlying the very large IBS and IBLL gains is difficult to trust without further controls. Most baselines are substantially adapted from classification, multimodal, or continuous-time formulations and are forced into four-bin discrete prediction, whereas DPsurV produces a continuous curve. Several baseline IBS values approach one, suggesting severe miscalibration or an implementation/protocol mismatch. The paper provides neither significance tests nor checks against authoritative implementations.

There are no ablations isolating the two prototype levels, GRFN evidence, mixture-evidential loss, regularizers, or belief/plausibility mixing coefficient. Consequently, the experiments cannot support the claimed causal importance of the proposed components. Sensitivity analysis is especially important because the limitations section identifies prototype count as critical and the selected component-prototype count varies by cohort and sometimes by fold.

The interpretability evidence is qualitative and appears limited to a selected example. The number of pathologists, annotation protocol, blinding, case-selection procedure, and inter-rater agreement are not reported. No quantitative localization, faithfulness test, perturbation analysis, or comparison with attention-based explanations is provided. Moreover, the within-slide min-max relative risk in Eq. 13 ignores mixture weights and uncertainty, is not an actual contribution decomposition of the final survival prediction, and is undefined when all component means coincide.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or seeds are supplied; patch magnification/size, tissue segmentation, train/validation selection, time-integration limits for IBS/IBLL, risk-score construction for C-index, number of likelihood bins, and the loss trade-off alpha are missing. Equations 4 and 34 are also dimensionally inconsistent unless the covariance is constrained to its diagonal, which is not clearly specified.

External validity is limited to retrospective TCGA data with no independent cohort, temporal validation, subgroup analysis, or robustness analysis for site and demographic shifts. The modest mean C-index gain over PANTHER (0.018), coupled with overlapping fold variability and a substantially worse BRCA result, does not justify broad generalizability claims.

Ethics and limitations: The manuscript lacks a clear ethics/data-governance statement and does not assess demographic bias. Its claim that conservative risk overestimation is clinically desirable is too strong: overestimation can also cause overtreatment and harm. Clinical-use language should be tempered until external validation, subgroup evaluation, and decision-utility studies are performed. Overall, these gaps leave the central uncertainty and interpretability claims insufficiently supported despite a promising method and encouraging predictive results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: combining uncertainty quantification with interpretable whole-slide-image survival prediction. The component-wise evidence formulation is intuitive and potentially useful for computational pathology.

The integration of morphology-oriented GMM components, prototype-based GRFN evidence, and prevalence-weighted evidence aggregation is a coherent combination of existing ideas. It provides a more structured explanation pathway than a conventional attention heatmap.

The empirical study covers five reasonably large public TCGA cohorts, uses site-stratified five-fold cross-validation, applies a common UNI2-h feature extractor, and reports discrimination and survival-probability metrics. DPsurv obtains the best reported mean C-index, IBS, and IBLL, with an additional CONCH experiment suggesting some robustness to the encoder.

The paper includes useful ablations, sensitivity analyses, computational-cost results, extra uncertainty baselines, and a pilot assessment by two pathologists. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges small-tumor failure cases, domain shift, possible interpretation bias, and the preliminary nature of the clinical assessment.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear, and its distinction among feature-, reasoning-, and decision-level explanations makes the intended contribution easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty-calibration claim is not adequately supported. Figures 3 and 7 estimate interval coverage using only uncensored patients. Conditioning evaluation on having an observed event creates selection bias under right censoring; valid coverage evaluation requires censoring-aware procedures or assumptions. IBS and IBLL assess the selected point survival curve, not calibration or correctness of the claimed epistemic/aleatoric decomposition. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that BPIs have calibrated coverage for the target survival population.

The mathematical description of the principal model is internally inconsistent. Proposition 3.5 says mixture belief and plausibility are sums over component-specific GRFNs, but Equations 11a–11d use a single unindexed mu, sigma, and h and omit the mixture weights and component summation. It is therefore unclear whether the implemented survival curve is computed from the mixture or an unsupported single-GRFN approximation.

The GMM representation is also underspecified or contradictory. Equation 4 assigns 2d+1 dimensions per component, implying diagonal variances, whereas Equation 36 estimates a full d-by-d covariance. Moreover, fitting a separate GMM to each slide can allow component identity drift despite common initialization; no matching constraint or empirical stability analysis establishes that component c retains a consistent semantic meaning across slides.

Several evaluation definitions are technically problematic. The stated C-index formula ignores censoring indicators and would treat censored times as observed events. The stated IBLL consists of logarithms and should be non-positive, yet the table reports positive values with lower declared better, indicating a missing sign or a mismatch between definition and implementation. The integration interval and censoring-estimator fitting protocol for IBS/IBLL are not specified, preventing verification and raising leakage concerns.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. Several classification or multimodal methods are substantially modified into four-bin, image-only survival models, while DPsurv uses a continuous GRFN-derived survival curve. The enormous calibration gaps may reflect these adaptations or objective/output differences. There are no significance tests or paired fold comparisons, and the discrimination improvement over BayesMIL is modest relative to the reported fold variability.

The evidence for interpretability is preliminary and does not justify claims of clinically meaningful or trustworthy reasoning. The component relative risk in Equation 13 is merely within-slide min-max normalization: it guarantees extrema, discards absolute risk, prevalence, and uncertainty, and is then broadcast over component assignments to create a spatial map. The expert study contains only 17 cases, provides no comparator, blinding protocol, annotation rubric, per-reader scores, or inter-rater agreement, and evaluates subjective coherence rather than prognostic faithfulness.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the slide decomposition closely follows PANTHER, while the GRFN survival machinery and evidence rules build directly on prior evidential survival work. The main novelty is their integration and component-level presentation, but the paper does not convincingly isolate gains due specifically to the proposed epistemic modeling.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract says code is available but gives no URL, and important details such as random seeds, patch/tissue preprocessing, exact metric implementation, evaluation time range, convergence settings, and component covariance parameterization are missing. Public datasets and a hyperparameter table help, but are insufficient to reproduce the unusually large calibration gains.

The ethics discussion is not appropriate for a clinical-prognosis paper: the impact statement asserts that no societal consequences need highlighting. Potential consequences include automation bias, subgroup/site performance disparities, misleading confidence estimates, and harm from clinical use without external or prospective validation. No demographic fairness analysis or external validation is presented.

strengths: Soundness: The component-wise GRFN formulation is motivated clearly, includes derivations, and is evaluated on five TCGA cohorts with five-fold cross-validation, ablations, sensitivity analyses, and a second feature extractor.

Presentation: The manuscript is visually polished and generally easy to follow; the overview and prototype visualizations communicate the intended feature-to-evidence-to-decision pipeline effectively.
Significance: Jointly addressing uncertainty and interpretability in WSI survival prediction is clinically relevant, and the reported average C-index of 0.704 is competitive.

Originality: Combining morphology-aware GMM components, component-specific prototypes, and evidential survival aggregation is a coherent new integration, even though its principal ingredients closely follow PANTHER and prior GRFN survival models.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges small-tumor failure cases, the absence of strong domain-shift evaluation, and the pilot nature of the pathologist study. weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of well-calibrated epistemic uncertainty is not adequately validated. IBS and IBLL are proper prediction scores rather than direct tests of epistemic uncertainty, while the interval-coverage plots discard every censored case without censoring correction. Because uncensoring depends on event time, this subset can give systematically biased coverage estimates.

Soundness: The belief/plausibility bounds are model-implied Dempster-Shafer quantities, but Proposition 3.2 effectively assumes that the unknown event-time law is compatible with the learned GRFN. The paper provides no identification, coverage guarantee, or empirical stress test establishing that these curves bound the true survival function. Thus the language of reliable or conservative uncertainty is stronger than the evidence supports.

Evaluation fairness: Most baselines are modified to four-bin discrete survival predictors, whereas DPsurv produces a continuous survival curve. The integration interval and numerical evaluation grid for IBS/IBLL are not specified. This mismatch is especially concerning because DPsurv's enormous gains are concentrated in IBS/IBLL, while C-index gains are modest relative to fold variability. Several baselines are also altered substantially, including removing UMSA's genomic input and adapting classification methods, without evidence that the adaptations are competitive.

Evaluation: No paired statistical tests or fold-level comparisons support the state-of-the-art claim. For example, the average C-index improvement over BayesMIL is only 0.030, with per-cohort standard deviations commonly between 0.05 and 0.11.

Interpretability: The proposed component-wise 'relative risk' is merely a within-slide min-max normalization of component means. It ignores mixture prevalence and uncertainty, is undefined when component means coincide, is not comparable across patients, and is not a standard relative risk or hazard ratio. Prototype visualizations therefore establish plausibility, not faithful causal or clinical attribution.

Interpretability study: Only 17 cases and two pathologists are used. The paper reports averaged ordinal scores but no rater-specific results, inter-rater agreement, rubric, controls, comparison with attention-based explanations, or statistical analysis. The asserted agreement between annotations and assignments is therefore weakly substantiated.

Method specification contains inconsistencies: covariance is written as a full matrix in the GMM equations but later represented as only d variance values; globally aligned patch prototypes are followed by per-slide EM without an explicit constraint preventing component-label drift; and the text alternates between treating h as epistemic uncertainty and as evidential precision, even though lower h corresponds to greater epistemic uncertainty.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The claimed code link is blank, and the manuscript omits split identifiers, random seeds, detailed WSI preprocessing and magnification, handling of multiple slides per patient, exact early-stopping rules, IBS/IBLL integration horizons, baseline adaptation details, and implementation details for the MC-dropout and ensemble comparisons. Table 9 also lacks cohort-wise results and uncertainty estimates.

Clinical generalization is not demonstrated: all experiments use retrospective TCGA cohorts, and site-stratified splitting is explicitly chosen to minimize train-test distribution differences. There is no external cohort, temporal validation, or robust out-of-domain test.

Ethics and limitations: The honest limitations discussion is a positive feature, but the generic impact statement is inadequate for a clinically framed model. The paper does not discuss demographic or site bias, consequences of erroneous risk estimates, governance of the pathologist evaluation, or safeguards against clinical deployment. These omissions do not create an immediate ethical violation, but they weaken the paper's claims of clinical trustworthiness.

Overall, the idea is promising and the presentation is polished, but unsupported uncertainty claims, biased/incomplete calibration validation, questionable baseline comparability, and insufficient reproducibility prevent others from reliably building on the result. These are central evidential problems warranting rejection rather than a minor revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: survival prediction from heterogeneous whole-slide images with both uncertainty quantification and clinically meaningful interpretation. Connecting morphology-aware components to component-level survival evidence is potentially useful for computational pathology.

The integration of prototype-guided GMM representations, component-specific Gaussian random fuzzy numbers, and evidence-level mixture aggregation is a coherent and moderately original combination. The component-wise construction is more transparent than a conventional single slide embedding or attention heatmap.

Evaluation covers five TCGA cancer cohorts using site-stratified five-fold cross-validation and a common UNI2-h feature extractor. DPsurv obtains the best reported average C-index (0.704), IBS (0.310), and IBLL (0.824), with reasonably consistent discrimination across cancers.

The paper includes useful ablations, prototype-number sensitivity analyses, a second feature extractor on UCEC, computational-cost results, qualitative visualizations, and a pilot assessment by two pathologists. The authors also provide an honest limitations section discussing small tumor regions, domain shift, interpretive bias, and the preliminary nature of clinical validation.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. The appendices provide derivations, initialization details, dataset sizes, baseline descriptions, hyperparameters, and additional examples. No major ethical concern is apparent because the experiments use public retrospective data, although deployment claims appropriately require further validation.
weaknesses: The central calibration claim is not adequately supported. Figure 3 evaluates interval coverage only among uncensored patients; this selected subset is generally not representative under censoring, and no inverse-censoring correction or censoring-aware coverage procedure is described. IBS and IBLL are proper predictive scores but do not by themselves establish calibration or validate the claimed epistemic uncertainty. Consequently, the evidence does not justify describing the intervals as reliably calibrated for the full survival population.

The interpretation of GRFN parameters is conceptually inconsistent. The manuscript calls h both a precision and a quantity representing epistemic uncertainty, while smaller similarity reduces h and is said to increase epistemic uncertainty. More fundamentally, Proposition 3.2 only states belief/plausibility bounds under an assumed compatible probability; it does not show that a learned GRFN bounds the true data-generating survival function. No OOD, sample-size, corruption, or other controlled experiment verifies that h actually tracks epistemic uncertainty separately from aleatoric uncertainty.

Experimental comparability and reporting contain consequential ambiguities. Most baselines are adapted to four-bin discrete survival prediction, whereas DPsurv produces a different continuous/evidential parameterization. The appendix inconsistently says PANTHER uses Cox loss and that it is adapted to discrete survival prediction. UMSA is evaluated after removing its genomic modality, and cited survival-specific uncertainty methods such as CTUSurv are not compared. Statistical significance tests are absent despite large fold-level variance.

The very large calibration-score improvements need stronger validation. Results without early stopping in Tables 2, 6, 7, and 9 differ substantially from the main results, sometimes being markedly better, but the criterion used to select K is not specified. Table 9 gives unusually poor MC-dropout and ensemble results without implementation details or matched base architectures. The C-index definition in Eq. 39 also omits the event indicator needed to define comparable pairs under censoring, while the reported positive, lower-is-better IBLL conflicts with the sign of Eq. 42.

The interpretability evidence remains preliminary and partly post hoc. Only 17 cases are scored, with no detailed sampling protocol, annotation rubric, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty on scores, or comparison against attention/prototype baselines. The component-wise relative-risk definition is a within-slide min-max normalization of mu: it necessarily assigns extrema, can be undefined when component means coincide, ignores mixture prevalence and uncertainty, and is not an actual decomposition of the final predicted risk. Thus the spatial maps demonstrate semantic plausibility rather than faithful causal or quantitative attribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the displayed code link is blank, and important details such as magnification and patch size, tissue preprocessing, event/censoring statistics, number of time bins B, metric integration interval, random seeds, model-selection metric, and complete MC-dropout/ensemble settings are missing. External-cohort validation is also absent, so robustness beyond TCGA and under clinically relevant domain shifts remains unresolved. These weaknesses affect the paper's central reliability claims and, in my assessment, outweigh its promising design and empirical discrimination results.
